claims.text: The proposed alloy has at least five elements, each at 5–35 at%, with Ti and Ni as the dominant constituents.
The baseline alloy contains no Mo and no significant refractory-element content.
Approximately 10 at% Mo will replace one minor element in the Ti–Ni-primary alloy.
Mo substitution will improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without Mo.
Mo addition will produce a dispersed network of fine Mo-rich precipitates or intermetallic phases in the matrix.
The Mo-rich precipitates will be thermally stable at 800–1000 °C.
Fine Mo-rich precipitates will hinder dislocation movement.
Mo-containing precipitates will stabilize or pin grain boundaries and inhibit grain-boundary sliding.
Precipitation strengthening and grain-boundary stabilization will reduce high-temperature creep.
Precipitation strengthening will maintain or increase yield strength at high temperature.
The Mo-modified alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in high-temperature yield strength relative to the baseline.
The Mo-modified alloy will exhibit statistically significant improvement in creep resistance relative to the baseline.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to Mo substitutions of about 5–10 at% while every alloying element remains within 5–35 at%.
The hypothesis is intended to apply during testing at 800–1000 °C under a controlled atmosphere.
Applicability depends on the microstructure remaining stable without formation of deleterious phases.
